{"id": "11:108/q10", "question": "What does the exception إِلَّا مَا شَآءَ رَبُّكَ exclude for Paradise's people?", "turns_on": "The dispute turns on whether exception changes the start or end of residence, adds duration or quality, states a hypothetical divine prerogative, or leaves its content undisclosed.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q10/p1", "position": "The time sinful monotheists spend in Hell before being brought into Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, Ibn ʿAbbās and others transmit this. Al-Ṭabarī prefers it because illā ordinarily marks a real exception; al-Ṭabrisī selects it. Abū Ḥayyān says late entrants did not begin with first entrants. A sound Anas report describes the Jahannamiyyūn brought out like charcoal; Abū Hurayra’s prophetic report applies both exceptions to them. Al-Samīn objects that Hell departure alone does not explain the blessed side; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects to reducing the exhaustive groups to sinners, while offering a general formulation involving the same people."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p2", "position": "They receive higher bliss beyond ordinary Paradise: divine pleasure, vision, nearness, or other gifts.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf cites divine approval and gifts beyond recompense; al-Bayḍāwī names vision and proximity; al-Nasafī calls them greater than Garden pleasures; Rāzī suggests elevation to the Throne or stations known only to God, citing 9:72. Some Companions hoped for such elevation and the Prophet approved. Elmalılı cites 9:72 and 75:22–23; Asad reports Rāzī and Manār on a greater reward. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn object that greater gifts do not interrupt residence."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p3", "position": "An interval before entry into the final abode: worldly life, grave, barzakh, gathering, judgment, or Resurrection Day.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysān and al-Qurṭubī list several stages; al-Balkhī prefers gathering, judgment or barzakh. Al-Māwardī specifically names Resurrection Day. Sāmarrāʾī reports fifty thousand years at the gathering and time until the reckoning finishes. Abū Ḥayyān favors an interval on Judgment Day; Rāzī rejects pre-entry intervals as outside residence; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says barzakh is preliminary lodging, not this final scene."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p4", "position": "A further unending duration, beyond the stated span, is added by God's will.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn Qutayba use illā as siwā; al-Ṭabarī’s grammarian invokes God's promise and the uncut gift. Al-Tirmidhī al-Ḥakīm takes the worldly span as the covenant term, followed by unlimited outcome. Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes disconnected exception from a possible ‘and’ reading; Rāzī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī object to the departure from ordinary wording."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p5", "position": "The exception expresses God's free power and grace: residence persists because He wills it, and He could have willed otherwise.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says bliss is gracious, not owed independently; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says power remains unrestricted while the uncut gift guarantees no expulsion. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuranyolu say the exception prevents treating mercy as a debt. Elmalılı says everlastingness is neither natural nor necessary in itself. Rāzī objects that a real exception is entailed by the syntax. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes God's duty to fulfill promises from His right to waive threats."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p6", "position": "The exception concerns other kinds of bliss, just as the preceding verse may refer to other kinds of punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj contrasts unmentioned delights with groaning in 11:106; al-Kashshāf gives cold, wrath and humiliation for Hell and divine approval for Paradise. Rāzī calls this a departure from the apparent sense; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the uncut gift proves duration, not kinds."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p7", "position": "God has willed them to remain forever; the exception is rhetorical, hypothetical, or leaves the precise decree to Him.", "reasons": "Abū Sinān and Abū Mālik read the following uncut gift as the answer; al-Ḥasan says the exception emphasizes the settled will. Qatāda and Abū Wāʾil leave its detail to God. Al-Qurṭubī compares 48:27's settled promise; Ibn ʿAbbās says He wills both groups to remain eternally."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p8", "position": "The specific exception is not disclosed; God alone knows what He wills.", "reasons": "Qatāda and Abū Wāʾil leave its outcome or wording to God; Ibn Zayd says Paradise's unending gift is disclosed but Hell's will is not. Ibn Qutayba's brief lexical note directs the duration and exception issue to al-Mushkil without another gloss; Rāzī's interlocutor asks whether a disputed reading is only a last resort and how the blessed clause can be handled."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p9", "position": "Some blessed people pass from Paradise into a higher state or new stage beyond it.", "reasons": "Bursevī describes a station beyond entry and exit, where primordial eternity appears in everlastingness, comparing saints' annihilation and distinguishing the people of beauty from majesty. Qāshānī describes selfless witnessing beyond garden states. Asad prefers a new higher stage for humanity; Kuranyolu attributes a similar view to him."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p10", "position": "The exception marks later entry by successive groups, including people of al-Aʿrāf.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Salām ibn al-Mustanīr describe companies arriving in sequence; Abū Ḥayyān says people of al-Aʿrāf or sinful believers begin after first entrants. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that the clause measures endpoint, not staggered starting points, citing 39:71 and 39:73."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p11", "position": "It may indicate an actual end to residence after the stated span.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this possibility for both groups; al-Rāzī infers Hell's termination from the gift's explicit reassurance only for Paradise. Al-Jishumī rejects termination of both abodes by consensus, and al-Burhān and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cite the unbroken gift against ending Paradise."}, {"id": "11:108/q10/p12", "position": "The blessed are monotheists, and the exception distinguishes them from polytheists.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this as a distinct fourth view resembling Abū Naḍra's."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q11", "question": "How is عَطَآءً construed?", "turns_on": "Whether the accusative confirms an implied act of giving, describes a state, or specifies the object of divine will.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q11/p1", "position": "It is an accusative verbal noun or cognate object supplied by the sense of God giving Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says the preceding promise implies ‘giving them bliss’; al-Qaṭāmī's poem supports a noun used for a verbal noun. Al-Samīn allows ism-maṣdar, loss of letters from iʿṭāʾ, or an implied verb, comparing 71:17. Al-Ālūsī prefers this parse; al-Bayḍāwī calls it emphatic."}, {"id": "11:108/q11/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial accusative qualifying the blessed or Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī gives it circumstantial force as well as verbal-noun force; al-Bayḍāwī takes it from Paradise; Elmalılı says it shows uninterrupted delights."}, {"id": "11:108/q11/p3", "position": "It specifies what God's will grants, including spiritual bliss.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports a specification of willing; Elmalılı says this directly makes the higher bliss uninterrupted; Abū al-Suʿūd says it can be the state of an implied object of divine will."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q12", "question": "What does غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍۢ mean?", "turns_on": "The lexical variants emphasize cessation, withholding, or diminution of the same lasting gift.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q12/p1", "position": "Uncut, unsevered and uninterrupted; the gift never ceases.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and others give this gloss. The root jadhdha means cut; Ibn Qutayba lists jadadta, jadhadta, jadhafta and jadafta; al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī cite al-Nābigha's armor-cutting poem. Al-Naḥḥās cites an unattributed poem. Al-Samīn connects jadhdh with jadd and cites al-Rāghib on cutting ground, cloth and the origin of jadīd. Al-Biqāʿī includes no break even for a moment; 56:33 and 41:8 provide parallels."}, {"id": "11:108/q12/p2", "position": "Not withheld or taken away.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives this second gloss; Ibn Zayd says the gift is not taken away; al-Qushayrī says blessings are neither severed nor withheld."}, {"id": "11:108/q12/p3", "position": "Not diminished at all.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan and al-Dāmghānī include absence of diminution; al-Biqāʿī says even a temporary reduction would count as severance."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q13", "question": "What does the closing promise عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍۢ establish?", "turns_on": "Whether the Paradise guarantee bears on Hell's fate by parallelism, asymmetry, or neither.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q13/p1", "position": "Paradise's reward and residence continue forever, so the exception does not end them.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Jishumī, al-Kashshāf, Ibn Kathīr, al-Burhān, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kuranyolu draw this inference. 56:33, 13:35, 16:96, and 41:8 are cited for unending provision. Wakiʿ calls Jahmiyya's rejection of these verses disbelief. The prophetic report says residents have no death, age, illness or suffering. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes promise-keeping from waiving a threat."}, {"id": "11:108/q13/p2", "position": "The different endings leave Hell's duration under God's will while assuring Paradise's unending gift.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says Hell's specific decree is not stated; Ibn Kathīr contrasts divine justice and wisdom in punishment with gracious assurance; al-Ālūsī says God may relieve some and leave others. Rāzī infers Hell's eventual termination from this asymmetry; Elmalılı rejects inferring punishment's general end from the promise to Paradise."}, {"id": "11:108/q13/p3", "position": "The lasting gift also proves everlasting punishment by pa

Al-Burhān rejects forcing both exceptions to the same nonliteral sense."}, {"id": "11:108/q13/p4", "position": "The closing wording comforts the saved and emphasizes permanence after the threat to the damned.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī explains its placement; al-Ālūsī notes that the preceding Hell passage warns and admonishes, hence the saved people's joy is not separately narrated."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q14", "question": "What do reports of Hell becoming empty say, and how are they understood?", "turns_on": "Whether the reports refer to all inhabitants, faithful sinners only, or transfer to another torment; source authors weigh their soundness against the promise of eternal punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q14/p1", "position": "A time will come when Hell is empty and its doors close, even after its inmates have remained for ages.", "reasons": "Reports are attributed to Ibn Masʿūd, Abū Hurayra and ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr; al-Ḥasan says even a sand-long stay has an end; al-Shaʿbī says Hell fills and decays sooner; Ibrāhīm calls this the most hopeful verse. Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports a resulting claim that Hell and its inhabitants perish."}, {"id": "11:108/q14/p2", "position": "If sound, emptying means no faithful sinners remain, while unbelievers remain eternally punished.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī gives this Sunni interpretation; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says reports concern the highest level reserved for sinful believers. Al-Kashshāf condemns reading ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr as denying unbelievers' eternal punishment, and al-Ālūsī cites consensus and decisive proofs. Ibn al-Jawzī calls some empty-Hell reports fabricated. Al-Kashshāf also criticizes Ibn ʿAmr for having fought ʿAlī."}, {"id": "11:108/q14/p3", "position": "Hell may be empty of those transferred from its fire to freezing or another torment.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf reconciles the clapping-door report with continued punishment this way; Rāzī objects that authentic reports make movement between heat and cold recurrent, not a single event after a set duration."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q15", "question": "Was the exception later abrogated?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception originally implied eventual termination; opponents cite the unsevered gift and other declarations of abiding.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q15/p1", "position": "Yes: later verses remove the exception and establish lasting Paradise, with a Medinan threat also closing hope of release from Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī cites 4:122 for Paradise in one transmission and 4:57 with 4:168 for both abodes in another."}, {"id": "11:108/q15/p2", "position": "No: the verse already secures Paradise, and there is no sound basis for abrogation.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the claim presumes an end absent from the wording and conflicts with other Meccan permanence statements; al-Ālūsī says decisive proofs of unbelievers' punishment make abrogation unnecessary."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q16", "question": "What inward meanings are given to the Garden, its heavens and earth, and the exception?", "turns_on": "Whether symbolic states describe ascent through the afterlife or a valid inward application distinct from the verse's apparent Resurrection scene.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q16/p1", "position": "The Garden is the soul's enjoyment of fulfilled desires; higher gardens of heart and spirit disclose God.", "reasons": "Qāshānī pairs the self's deprivation and gratification with later states of heart and spirit, then describes annihilation in divine unity and selfless witnessing. Al-Ālūsī likewise moves from the soul's garden to witnessing attributes and spiritual vision. Bursevī contrasts ascent by works with divine attraction beyond duality."}, {"id": "11:108/q16/p2", "position": "Garden and Fire can signify God's and Satan's authority embodied in bliss and torment, with movement governed by faith and conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī accepts this as an inward meaning but rejects it as the apparent sense of a passage about Resurrection's distinctive terrors."}, {"id": "11:108/q16/p3", "position": "The heavens mean spirits and hearts, while earth means souls and embodied humanity.", "reasons": "Bursevī reports this from the people of inward interpretation."}, {"id": "11:108/q16/p4", "position": "The exception can point to a station beyond Paradise's ordinary entry and exit, in which the secret of eternity appears.", "reasons": "Bursevī's oral teaching describes a final disclosure unlike earlier states, likens it to saints' annihilation, and relates the people of beauty and majesty and the perfected knowers across worldly life, barzakh and afterlife. He also reports differing numbers of spiritual barriers crossed after death, with the cited excerpt unfinished."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q17", "question": "How does this verse connect the final judgment to the preceding and following passages?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q17/p1", "position": "It contrasts God's freedom to punish or relieve in 11:107 with the assured gift to Paradise's people here.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr links God's justice, wisdom and will to 21:23; al-Burhān says the paired endings explain gracious rescue and uninterrupted gift; al-Ālūsī notes the Hell passage's warning aim."}, {"id": "11:108/q17/p2", "position": "It completes the sequence of gathering, division, then lasting destinations.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī and Kuranyolu relate it to the gathering in 11:103 and two groups' faith and deeds; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī treats the preceding Hell duration and this Garden duration as parallel settled residences."}, {"id": "11:108/q17/p3", "position": "The contrast connects worldly choices to the destinations: seekers of this life meet Fire; humble believers meet Paradise.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites 11:15–16 and 11:23, while Kuranyolu reads outcomes according to faith and deeds."}, {"id": "11:108/q17/p4", "position": "The passage's afterlife garden is final reward, unlike preliminary garden or fire in the grave.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 3:169–170 and 23:99–100 for the barzakh's intermediate state and contrasts it with the final accounting and everlasting reward."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q18", "question": "How do the exception here and the preceding exception for Hell compare?", "turns_on": "Whether the paired clauses share a single referent or require different effects because Paradise's gift is explicitly unbroken.", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q18/p1", "position": "They need different outcomes: no one leaves Paradise once admitted, while the Hell exception may still permit release.", "reasons": "Rāzī invokes consensus that no Paradise entrant later leaves for Hell. Al-Ṭabrisī extends the earlier exception proposals only where compatible with permanent Paradise. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the Paradise gift promises no removal, unlike the Hell clause of unfettered will; he objects to Abu Majliz's separate explanation as breaking contextual unity and treating pardoned persons as wretched."}, {"id": "11:108/q18/p2", "position": "Both clauses preserve God's sovereignty; the closing phrases show what He actually decrees for each group.", "reasons": "The uncut gift assures Paradise, while ‘He does what He wills’ in 11:107 can include mercy. Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes God's power; Abū Jaʿfar's report points to the different endings."}, {"id": "11:108/q18/p3", "position": "The Hell exception can refer to other punishments or to a pause after worldly and grave torment, while Paradise remains assured.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf speaks of extreme cold; Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭūsī's reported view puts Hell during the world's span including graves, with a pause until resurrection. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the latter repeats a strained ‘other than’ analysis."}, {"id": "11:108/q18/p4", "position": "They can concern the same sinful monotheists: release from Hell there and their earlier absence from Paradise here.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī formulates this for the exhaustive final groups; al-Burhān keeps the Hell exception's ordinary sense as deliverance. Abū Majliz instead allows pardon before Hell and a different Paradise interval."}, {"id": "11:108/q18/p5", "position": "Abū Majliz takes the first exception as those pardoned before Hell and the second as sinners later entering Paradise.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this disrupts the two verses' unity and that those pardoned through deeds or intercession were happy from the outset."}]}
{"id": "11:108/q19", "question": "How does repeated wording in the Paradise clause work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:108/q19/p1", "position": "Repetition in a genitive or prepositional construction can confirm the earlier phrase, even when separated.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān cites transmitted instances including pronouns, repeated lammā and repeated annakum; al-Ṣaffār rejects the Kūfan rule against separating an emphatic element. Al-Itqān also notes emphasis by synonyms."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q01", "question": "What force does فَلَوْلَا have here?", "turns_on": "Whether the particle is read as reproach with an implied negative, a wish, or its broader conditional use; the universal hallā attribution is tested against other Qur'anic instances.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q01/p1", "position": "It asks reproachfully why earlier communities had no people forbidding corruption; the question implies their scarcity or absence.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba and Burhan say lawlā without an answer means hallā, with a past verb expressing reproach; Ibn Qutayba cites 9:122, 6:43, 56:86 and a poet. Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn ʿAbbās take its implication as 'there were not,' comparing 10:98. Al-Rummānī allows either reproach or question. Burhan prefers exhortation because Ubayy reads fahlā; its reproach still implies nonoccurrence. Al-Ṭabarī points to unheeded signs, proofs and consequences. Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyā

Asad renders it 'alas.'"}, {"id": "11:116/q01/p2", "position": "It is a wish that earlier people of virtue had existed.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf gives 'would that there had been'; al-Jishumī reports analysis as law of wishing joined to lā, by analogy with hallā in censure."}, {"id": "11:116/q01/p3", "position": "Every Qur'anic lawlā means hallā except its occurrence in al-Ṣāffāt.", "reasons": "Attributed to al-Khalīl by al-Rāzī; al-Kashshāf, al-Samīn and al-Rāzī reject the universal claim, citing contrary examples at 68:49, 48:25 and 17:74; al-Samīn identifies 37:143 as the purported exception."}, {"id": "11:116/q01/p4", "position": "In its original conditional use, lawlā means 'if it were not for' an existing impediment.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī illustrates it with disobedience preventing good treatment; this explains the particle's broader range rather than making that conditional sense the verse's local reading."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q02", "question": "How is the opening read in the report from Ubayy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q02/p1", "position": "Ubayy's transmitted reading opens 'Had there been among the generations before you.'", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports Ubayy saying the Prophet taught him this wording; Burhan also invokes Ubayy's fahlā wording to support the exhortative force."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q03", "question": "How do the opening words fit grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether kāna is complete or deficient, and whether the focus falls on the existence of virtuous people or their act of forbidding.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q03/p1", "position": "Kāna is complete, with ūlū baqiyya its subject; the prepositional phrases locate it among former generations.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says min al-qurūn may attach to complete kāna or be circumstantial to ūlū, while min qablikum qualifies al-qurūn. Al-Ālūsī reports partitive min and a circumstance or adjective for min qablikum; he notes objection that this parse focuses on existence rather than forbidding, while usage can focus on the qualification. His lute simile illustrates that added qualification."}, {"id": "11:116/q03/p2", "position": "Kāna can be incomplete, with yanhawna its predicate and min al-qurūn an implied circumstantial phrase.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn calls it semantically weaker and says most grammarians do not let deficient kāna govern the prepositional phrase here."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q04", "question": "Who are the earlier قُرُون?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q04/p1", "position": "They are earlier communities, especially the destroyed peoples previously narrated, including Noah's people, ʿĀd and Thamūd.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān name Noah's people, ʿĀd and Thamūd; al-Biqāʿī calls them once powerful destroyed peoples. Ibn ʿĀshūr glosses qurūn as nations or communities and points to his discussion at 6:1. Asad points to his note at 6:5."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q05", "question": "What span does a qarn denote?", "turns_on": "The reported span of a generation; Ibn ʿAṭiyya favors the century estimate using a Prophetic report.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q05/p1", "position": "A people sharing a long period, reckoned here as a hundred years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers a hundred years on the Prophetic report that no one alive on a given night would remain after a century; Ibn ʿUmar says this marks the end of that generation."}, {"id": "11:116/q05/p2", "position": "A generation may be reckoned as eighty years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this estimate among alternatives."}, {"id": "11:116/q05/p3", "position": "A generation may be reckoned as thirty years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this estimate among alternatives."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q06", "question": "What are أُو۟لُوا۟ بَقِيَّةٍ?", "turns_on": "Whether baqiyya emphasizes retained virtue, discernment, religious obedience and self-preservation, a small remnant, or lasting benefit; many sources combine these senses.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q06/p1", "position": "People of virtue, goodness and praiseworthy excellence, the best remaining members of a community.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj cites the idiom 'a person has baqiyya'; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr explain that people keep their best possessions. Al-Kashshāf, Abū Ḥayyān and Ibn ʿĀshūr cite a Ḥamāsa line and the proverb about hidden things and human remnants. Al-Jishumī relates it to what remains and preservation; al-Biqāʿī adds gathering, strength, endurance, guarding and quality. Ibn al-Jawzī distinguishes baqāʾ enduring successively from baqiyya remaining after companions vanish, and reports Arabs using baqā for baqiya. Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 2:248 and his discussion of enduring good in Shuʿayb's speech."}, {"id": "11:116/q06/p2", "position": "People of discernment, reason, resolve and religious firmness who heed God's proofs.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī grounds the sense in reflection on God's admonitions and the stakes of belief; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān call them steadfast survivors as institutions weaken; al-Biqāʿī adds vigilance for benefit. Al-Ṭabrisī stresses God's gifts of reason, messengers and proofs."}, {"id": "11:116/q06/p3", "position": "People possessing religion, obedience and fear of God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās says 'religion'; Ibn Qutayba adds moral firmness. Al-Zajjāj also offers obedience; al-Asamm and Abū Muslim describe fearing punishment and guarding against Hell. Al-Zamakhsharī and followers derive baqiyya from baqwā, akin to taqiyya/taqwā, preserving oneself from divine anger."}, {"id": "11:116/q06/p4", "position": "A small surviving number of people.", "reasons": "Al-Damghānī and Ibn al-Jawzī report this sense; al-Jishumī transmits Abū ʿAlī's more specific 'remnant of the elders,' asking why none persisted despite numerous messengers and proofs."}, {"id": "11:116/q06/p5", "position": "People blessed with enduring good or benefit.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī includes blessing among glosses. Ibn ʿĀshūr's linked discussion of Shuʿayb contrasts lasting divine reward with transient gains (19:76), cites 2:248 for preserved precious good, and explains that rightful earnings protect social order while wrongful seizure and ingratitude invite loss; he cites the Farewell Pilgrimage's inviolability of blood and property and Ibn ʿAṭāʾ Allāh on gratitude preserving blessings."}, {"id": "11:116/q06/p6", "position": "A virtuous community among earlier Mosaic and Christian adherents, serving what endures and helping others.", "reasons": "Elmalılı gives this specific historical identification."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q07", "question": "How is بَقِيَّةٍ read and derived?", "turns_on": "The vowels, yāʾ weight and derivation, with some forms tied to baqiya 'remain' and another to baqāhu 'watch or await.'", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q07/p1", "position": "The familiar baqiyya has a geminated yāʾ and can be an intensive adjective or a noun of preservation.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī relates it to preserving; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn describe an intensive feminine active adjective for select people. {"id": "11:116/q08", "question": "What does their forbidding corruption entail?", "turns_on": "Whether 'corruption' is specified chiefly as unbelief and sins or also as damaged social conditions.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q08/p1", "position": "They warn against unbelief, idolatry, disobedience and accompanying sins.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī specifies warnings to sinners and disbelievers; Ibn ʿAbbās includes shirk, violation of God's rights and disobedience. {"id": "11:116/q10", "question": "What does فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ attach to?", "turns_on": "Whether the location is governed by the verbal noun or is an implicit circumstantial qualification.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q10/p1", "position": "It attaches to the verbal noun 'corruption.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn notes that an article-marked verbal noun can govern objects, so it can govern an adverbial phrase."}, {"id": "11:116/q10/p2", "position": "It is an omitted circumstantial modifier of 'corruption.'", "reasons": "Al-Samīn offers this alternative."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q11", "question": "How does إِلَّا قَلِيلًۭا function?", "turns_on": "Whether lawlā retains affirmative exhortation or implies negation; the nominative can be analyzed as a substitute or as an adjective depending on the construction.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q11/p1", "position": "It is a disconnected exception: nevertheless a few of those rescued did forbid corruption.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī compare Jonah's people at 10:98; al-Ṭabarī also mentions 2:83. {"id": "11:116/q12", "question": "What does مِّمَّنْ أَنجَيْنَا مِنْهُمْ mean grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the preposition identifies all the saved with the forbiders or selects a subset of the saved.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q12/p1", "position": "Min explains the few: the rescued people were precisely those who forbade corruption.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī cites 7:165, followed by al-Nasafī and al-Ālūsī. {"id": "11:116/q13", "question": "Who were the few saved forbiders?", "turns_on": "Whether the few are prophetic followers generally, prophets as well, or specifically Jonah's people.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q13/p1", "position": "The small number of prophetic followers, believers and people of truth in earlier nations.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan names Noah, Hūd and Ṣāliḥ with their believers, citing 11:48; Ibn Jurayj and Qatāda stress the few in every people. {"id": "11:116/q14", "question": "Why does the verse say أَنجَيْنَا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q14/p1", "position": "It highlights beneficial rescue that encourages forbidding corruption.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says najjaynā would suggest gradual deliverance and obscure the point; Ibn ʿĀshūr links admonition, repentance and salvation."}]}
{"id": "11:116/q15", "question": "Who are ٱلَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا۟?", "turns_on": "Whether wrongdoing here points narrowly to failure to forbid evil or broadly to the active corrupting majority.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q15/p1", "position": "Those who abandoned the duty to forbid corruption, thus wronging themselves.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī call this a central religious duty; al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī tie the relative phrase to the preceding few. {"id": "11:116/q16", "question": "How is وَٱتَّبَعَ read?", "turns_on": "The active or passive morphology, with the passive requiring an understood recompense.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q16/p1", "position": "The common reading is active ittabaʿa, 'the wrongdoers followed.'", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid says Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr double the tāʾ, as do ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī here though they use cut or hamzated forms for other cited verbs. {"id": "11:116/q17", "question": "How does وَٱتَّبَعَ connect to what precedes?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause advances the narrative by coordination, gives a simultaneous circumstance, or stands independently.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q17/p1", "position": "It coordinates with an implied statement that the few forbade corruption while the others failed and followed desires.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Samīn supply the implied clause; al-Ālūsī notes a linkage problem if coordinated directly with nahaw and reports fixes such as supplying 'their counterparts' or making nahaw independent. {"id": "11:116/q18", "question": "What is مَآ أُتْرِفُوا۟ فِيهِ that the wrongdoers followed?", "turns_on": "Whether mā names enjoyed goods and desires, the consequence of that indulgence, or a reported alternative gloss.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q18/p1", "position": "Worldly ease, wealth, power, pleasures and status, preferred to duty and the afterlife.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ stresses familiar pleasure and preference for this life; al-Ṭabarī synthesizes pleasure, arrogance, disbelief, rebellion and obstructing God's path. {"id": "11:116/q19", "question": "What does the root of أُتْرِفُوا۟ convey?", "turns_on": "Whether insolence belongs to the word's lexical sense or is an effect of luxury in context.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q19/p1", "position": "Luxury, blessing, ease and expansion in prosperity; a mutraf is pampered or made indulgent by comfort.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī defines the person as raised in luxury and fed pleasures; al-Wāḥidī cites a comfortable child; Ibn ʿArafa says a mutraf is left free to do as he wishes. {"id": "11:116/q20", "question": "How is مَآ أُتْرِفُوا۟ فِيهِ parsed?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of fīhi and whether mā denotes a thing, an action, an omitted recompense, or a cause.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q20/p1", "position": "Mā is relative, referring to the luxuries or blessings in which they were indulged.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Taqrīb argue that fīhi refers back to mā; al-Samīn finds this more apparent on the passive reading. {"id": "11:116/q21", "question": "What does وَكَانُوا۟ مُجْرِمِينَ say about them?", "turns_on": "Whether criminality is specified as disbelief or as wider persistent wrongdoing, including ingratitude.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q21/p1", "position": "They were unbelievers or polytheists.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and al-Baghawī explicitly gloss criminals as unbelievers; al-Jishumī reports al-Aṣamm's polytheists; al-Ālūsī notes this is the graver offense."}, {"id": "11:116/q21/p2", "position": "They persisted in sins, neglecting correction and gratitude, beyond the pursuit of luxury.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf says crime can attach to indulgence as ingratitude or to desire-following; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report additional crimes beyond failure to forbid. {"id": "11:116/q22", "question": "How does وَكَانُوا۟ مُجْرِمِينَ connect grammatically?", "turns_on": "Which earlier clause receives the coordination, and whether the final clause is a grammatical parenthesis, circumstance, or explanatory judgment.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q22/p1", "position": "It coordinates with 'followed,' stating a further or resultant action.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī give this ordinary parse; al-Bursevī says the two clauses together explain the destroyed nations' crime. {"id": "11:116/q23", "question": "What duty does the verse establish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q23/p1", "position": "People should enjoin good, forbid corruption and respond to wrongdoing; neglect can expose a whole community to punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī infers the duty from censure and rescue. {"id": "11:116/q24", "question": "Why were earlier peoples destroyed, and who is spared?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q24/p1", "position": "Widespread unbelief and neglected correction, together with indulgence and other crimes, brought ruin; reforming believers were spared.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī distinguishes absence of forbiders as first cause and indulgence as second. {"id": "11:116/q25", "question": "How does this verse connect to its context and later audience?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q25/p1", "position": "It draws the lesson from the destroyed peoples' stories and urges the present community to maintain reform.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī connects it to 11:115's patience and the difficulty of persuading entrenched opponents, including imitators in worship and those disputing Moses' guidance. {"id": "11:116/q26", "question": "What do the cited poetic forms mean?", "turns_on": "The derivation of a poetic word cited while explaining affluent people.", "positions": [{"id": "11:116/q26/p1", "position": "Al-mumtād is the person asked for help; māda-hu means 'he asked him.'", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabrisī gloss the poetic form this way; al-Ṭabrisī's line about spoiled leaders' heads is cited in discussion of luxury."}, {"id": "11:116/q26/p2", "position": "Al-mumtād derives from māda yamīdu.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda gives this alternative derivation for the cited verse."}]}

{"id": "13:9/q01", "question": "What do the unseen and the witnessed designate?", "turns_on": "Whether the contrast is drawn by sensory access, privacy, existence, creaturely knowledge, time, or inward capacity; several sources treat these as instances of a comprehensive pair.", "positions": [{"id": "13:9/q01/p1", "position": "What lies beyond creatures' perception and what is present to their senses.", "reasons": "Muqatil includes the fetus while hidden in the womb and when visible, as well as everything else. Ibn Abbas in Wahidi and Razi, al-Rummani in Biqai, and Nasafi frame the contrast relative to creatures. Jishumi, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur specify sensory perception; Bursevi includes concealed knowledge, secrets, the afterlife, perceptible beings and the world. Wahidi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Ibn Ashur explain that abstract or verbal nouns stand for the absent and witnessed things; Ibn Ashur calls shahada passive in sense and cites 69:38–39.
